claim: PRC political negotiations commonly progress from relationship and agenda construction, through extended assessment, to a brief agreement-making phase and subsequent implementation bargaining.
evidence_type: Interview-derived synthesis; process diagram; selected memcon excerpts and memoir cases as reproduced by Solomon.
historical_anchor: Shanghai Communiqué negotiations, 1971–1972; normalization agreement, 1978; Taiwan arms-sales communiqué, 1981–1982.
test: Reconstruct dated interactions before applying stage labels. Measure order, overlap, repetition, and the duration of each proposed phase across successful, failed, and suspended negotiations. Test whether this sequence distinguishes PRC cases from counterpart practice or simply describes bargaining generally.
caveat: The chapter selects a few major agreements and repeatedly reuses them. The endgame admits abortion or continued bargaining. Cultural and institutional interpretations are not independently established by the regularity of a reconstructed sequence. Do not count repeated references to one episode as independent cases.

claim: PRC officials try to channel important negotiations through sympathetic foreign decision makers with senior access, sometimes bypassing or separating less congenial officials and advisers.
evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; narrative reconstruction of personnel preferences; commercial anecdotes; author inference.
historical_anchor: Mao–Nixon, February 21, 1972; Chinese preference for Kissinger conveyed through intermediaries in early 1971; Vance–Huang Hua, September 28, 1977; subsequent Brzezinski channel.
test: Code requested participants, actual attendance, access to the top decision maker, channels excluded, and policy changes after rerouting. Distinguish routine protocol from unusual exclusion and test whether the preferred interlocutor actually grants more favorable terms.
caveat: Solomon acknowledges that governments generally prefer friendly counterparts. Presidential access, substantive anti-Soviet alignment, and decision authority are practical explanations alongside guanxi. Physical isolation examples are principally commercial and should not automatically be generalized to summit diplomacy.

claim: Hosting negotiations and managing hospitality, protocol, timing, and uncertainty can give PRC officials influence over visitors' mood, fatigue, and perceived control.
evidence_type: Kissinger memoir passages; participant impressions; visit anecdotes; narrative comparison with older adversarial encounters.
historical_anchor: Kissinger's July and October 1971 visits; October 1975 communiqué discussions before Ford's visit; Nixon's staged Ming Tombs encounter and Ford's incorrectly selected university song.
test: Compare venues, control over schedules, delegation support, fatigue reports, and concessions. Seek documentation of intentional scheduling pressure. Test whether equivalent arrangements abroad or improved communications alter the pattern and whether repeated visitors become less susceptible.
caveat: The book gives practical reasons for Beijing venues, including communications and access to decision makers. It records gaffes and visitor suspicion. Kissinger expressly could not distinguish tactical delay from leadership review in July 1971; perceived manipulation is not proof of intent.

claim: PRC negotiators seek advantageous agenda wording and sequencing, and may withhold discussion of other issues to press a priority demand or protect relationships with allies.
evidence_type: Memcon and intermediary-message excerpts; older negotiator memoirs; author reconstruction of agenda bargaining.
historical_anchor: Stoessel–Lei, January 20 and February 20, 1970; Kissinger–Hilaly messages, December 1970–May 1971; Zhou–Kissinger, July 9 and 11, 1971; unsuccessful pressure on Ford in 1975.
test: Record each side's initial agenda, changes, excluded topics, reasons given, and substantive outcome. Compare public and private agendas. Test whether topic linkage extracts concessions, stalls other cooperation, or protects an alliance without changing the counterpart's priority position.
caveat: The final normalization dialogue included the broader security issues Washington sought. Agenda pressure failed to secure normalization under Ford. The chapter also attributes agenda precision to narrow instructions and preparation requirements, not only deliberate manipulation.

claim: PRC political negotiators favor broad principles and flexible political documents, subsequently invoking those formulations to constrain the counterpart while retaining discretion over concrete arrangements.
evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; communiqué descriptions; Freeman's 1975 analysis cited by Solomon; author interpretation of agreement form.
historical_anchor: Deng–Bush, May 8, 1982; Huang Hua–Woodcock, July 7, 1978; Vance–Huang Hua, October 3, 1978; Shanghai and normalization communiqués; Zhao Ziyang's 1983 policy statement.
test: Compare opening principles with final provisions, document type, specificity, enforcement arrangements, and later assertions of obligation. Include technically detailed negotiations and formal treaties. Identify when principles are declined, reinterpreted, or set aside and whether compromise still occurs.
caveat: Solomon concedes agreements apparently inconsistent with early principles and American refusals to accept Chinese formulations. Relationship trust, uncertainty reduction, and tactical flexibility are competing explanations. A unilateral claim that a principle was violated is not proof of a mutually accepted obligation.

claim: PRC negotiators often seek a comprehensive account of the counterpart's position before revealing their own, even when the host–guest justification changes with the venue.
evidence_type: Direct memcon excerpts; narrative descriptions of negotiating exchanges; explicit exception in footnote 21.
historical_anchor: Zhou–Kissinger, July 9, 1971; Huang Hua–Woodcock, July 5 and July 14, 1978; Geng–Brown, January 7, 1980; Kissinger–Qiao, October 8, 1976.
test: Code who presents the first substantive offer, who asks for further detail, whether presentation is reciprocal, and when Chinese instructions appear fixed. Compare informational advantage with the practical need to obtain a documented foreign position for superiors.
caveat: Footnote 21 says Chinese officials may present first when tasked with establishing a principle or limiting discussion. The behavior is an information-seeking convention, not sufficient evidence of a unique national characteristic or of concessions obtained.

claim: PRC officials sometimes use underspecified formulations, analogies, indirect signals, or apparent misunderstanding to elicit a concrete response while limiting their own immediate commitment.
evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; memoir-based narrative; author interpretations of symbolism; one short subsection without a developed example.
historical_anchor: Stoessel–Lei Yang, February 20, 1970; Mao–Kissinger and Zhou–Kissinger, November 12–14, 1973; Zhou–Nixon, February 23, 1972; Ji Chaozhu–U.S. Embassy Officer, March 2, 1982.
test: Preserve literal Chinese and English wording before assigning a hidden meaning. Compare the counterpart's interpretation with later clarification, instructions, or offers. Test ambiguity against genuine uncertainty, translation problems, or limited authorization, and record unsuccessful or missed signals.
caveat: The chapter sometimes marks these meanings as conjectural. Its playing-dumb subsection lacks a dated illustrative case. Cultural explanations of indirection do not exclude ordinary exploratory bargaining, and both sides can overinterpret symbolism.

claim: Trusted intermediaries and lower-level or informal channels can convey sensitive positions, test ideas, and insulate senior leaders from direct confrontation.
evidence_type: Intermediary-message and memcon excerpts; official-channel descriptions; one explicitly personal recollection.
historical_anchor: Kissinger–Hilaly, December 9, 1970; Pakistan's role in the opening; Haig–Zhang Wenjin, September 22, 1981; Allen–Chai, October 2, 1981; Zhang–Hummel, December 4 and 22, 1981.
test: Map senders, carriers, audiences, authority, deniability, and subsequent incorporation into official positions. Compare intermediary selection with available alternatives. Test whether the channel reduces confrontation, communicates genuine flexibility, or simply duplicates the formal position.
caveat: Trust and guanxi coexist with secrecy, access, common interests, and availability. Footnote 36 explicitly compares informal exchanges with U.S.–Soviet practice. A reported private message does not establish authorized policy unless its provenance can be verified.

claim: Humor, self-deprecation, and acknowledgment of minor errors can build rapport or preempt criticism, making later changes in tone more salient to foreign counterparts.
evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; Nixon and Kissinger memoir impressions; American interview recollections.
historical_anchor: Mao–Nixon, February 21, 1972; Deng's apology to George Bush in the Deng–Kissinger record, October 19, 1975; Kissinger–Qiao, November 13, 1972.
test: Trace changes in conversational tone, participant perceptions, and substantive bargaining in the same relationship. Compare first-time and experienced counterparts and different Chinese officials. Seek evidence connecting rapport to an identifiable concession rather than treating personal warmth as success.
caveat: Politeness, sincere error correction, personality, and shared humor are alternatives to calculated influence. The chapter's comparisons with Soviet humor are subjective and do not independently establish national cultural differences.

claim: PRC leaders use relations with third powers and rival foreign political figures to advertise alternatives, influence the counterpart's sense of dependence, and improve their bargaining position.
evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; contemporary event narratives; strategic interpretation, including explicitly conditional reasoning about 1969.
historical_anchor: Zhou–Kissinger, July 10–11, 1971; Deng–Kissinger, November 26, 1974; Mao–Kissinger, October 21, 1975; Kissinger–Huang Zhen, August 18, 1976; Reagan's meetings with PRC leaders, April 27, 1984.
test: Establish the alternative relationship's independent value, its timing relative to bargaining, explicit references to it, and counterpart responses. Compare genuine policy shifts with demonstrative gestures and distinguish domestic political rivals from international alternatives.
caveat: The proposed role of the March 1969 clashes in creating a wider coalition is conditional in Solomon's account. Domestic politics and genuine security interests also explain third-party actions. The Soviet helicopter-release footnote expressly leaves its internal dynamics unresolved.

claim: PRC officials may delay substantive movement until leadership conditions or the wider strategic context permit a more favorable agreement, preserving talks in the meantime.
evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; historical narrative; informal comments as reported by the author; retrospective causal interpretation.
historical_anchor: Vance's August 1977 Beijing visit; Huang Hua–Woodcock, November 14, 1977; Pu Shouchang–Hummel, March 18, 1982; Zhang Zai–Freeman, March 22, 1982; Pu Shouchang–Freeman, March 24, 1982.
test: Reconstruct periods of inactivity against changes in instructions, leadership authority, substantive positions, and external conditions. Identify evidence that an acceptable agreement existed but was deliberately deferred. Compare deliberate waiting with bureaucratic processing or irreconcilable interests.
caveat: Observed slowness does not identify its cause. The chapter relies partly on hindsight and foreign officials' interpretations of internal politics; apparent rigidity may reflect substantive preference rather than leadership conflict or a calculated delay.

claim: PRC negotiators can obtain partial agreements while explicitly reserving unresolved positions, and can preserve compromise options through wording that avoids a conspicuous reversal.
evidence_type: Agreement and memcon descriptions; interpretive discussion of credibility; strategic analogy without a standalone example.
historical_anchor: Unilateral paragraphs in the Shanghai Communiqué; Deng–Woodcock, December 15, 1978; Hua Guofeng's unilateral statement following normalization.
test: List issues settled, deferred, expressly reserved, or left ambiguous. Track whether later demands invoke those reservations and whether deferral stabilizes cooperation or increases leverage. Compare public rigidity with actual draft revisions and compromises.
caveat: An explicit reservation is not concealment and does not show agreement on the reserved issue. Solomon admits that normalization was not a fully specified plan and contrasts political credibility concerns with commercial retreats. The Sun-tzu explanation is an analogy, not demonstrated transmission of a military rule.

claim: PRC negotiators can increase pressure through explicit threats, limited costly confrontations, or expanded demands, with the form and willingness to act changing as the relationship develops.
evidence_type: Narrative comparison across negotiation phases; American interview assessments; memcon-anchored cultural-exchange dispute.
historical_anchor: Relative absence of overt threats before 1979 versus their prominence in the 1981 arms-sales dispute; Habib–Han Xu exchanges, March 19, 20, 23, and 25, 1975, preceding cancellation of a performing-arts tour.
test: Record each threatened condition, consequence, material cost, implementation, retreat, and negotiated outcome. Test whether progressively disclosed requirements were new demands. Compare relationship stage, issue salience, domestic politics, and relative power as explanations for escalation.
caveat: Solomon states both that threats were sometimes abandoned and that some were carried out. The 1975 tour failed, and its factional purpose is disputed within the chapter. Neither threat issuance nor a canceled exchange proves bargaining success.

claim: Foreign officials invested in a positive relationship with China may receive concentrated pressure because PRC leaders expect them to work hardest to preserve it.
evidence_type: Memcon and letter excerpts; narrative accounts of visits; author interpretation of reputational and relational incentives.
historical_anchor: Kissinger's treatment during the 1975 Ford-visit preparations; Bush's August 1980 visit; Deng–Bush, May 8, 1982; Zhao–Bush letter, January 20, 1981.
test: Compare pressure on established friends and skeptical officials facing the same issue, controlling for office, access, and negotiating authority. Measure whether friendly status brings greater access, harsher demands, more concessions, or improved ability to resist pressure.
caveat: Guanxi is Solomon's principal cultural explanation, but reputational investment and expected policy influence offer practical alternatives. The chapter also reports PRC weakness in reaching hostile Americans, so concentrated contact may reflect access limitations rather than superior manipulation.

claim: PRC leaders can invoke popular sentiment or the political vulnerability of accommodating officials as a limit on their flexibility and a reason for the counterpart to concede.
evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; author interpretation of domestic political constraints; competing explanations of the 1975 cultural dispute.
historical_anchor: Deng–Haig, June 16, 1981; Deng–Mondale, November 22, 1981; 1975 performing-arts dispute; post-Mao references to public feelings on Taiwan.
test: Compare claims of domestic constraint with available evidence of elite disagreement, institutional authorization, public mobilization, and later policy change. Distinguish a real constraint, selective presentation of one, and an unsupported bargaining assertion.
caveat: Solomon explicitly cannot determine whether some warnings are hollow and compares them with American invocation of Congress. The asserted change in popular influence under Deng is a period-specific interpretation, not a general model of how public opinion controls PRC policy.

claim: Negotiating tone varies with individuals, assigned roles, senior instructions, and domestic circumstances; alternating harder and more accommodating presentations can affect expectations about compromise.
evidence_type: Memoir and interview impressions; memcon-based personality sketches; comparison of the same official across periods.
historical_anchor: Huang Hua's accommodating role in Kissinger's early exchanges versus his harder presentation in 1978–1982; Zhou's deference to Mao; Qiao's October 1975 and October 8, 1976, encounters with Kissinger.
test: Compare each individual's behavior across roles, issues, and leadership periods, and different negotiators operating under the same authority. Code tone separately from actual offer changes. Seek evidence of instructions before attributing a hard–soft pairing to orchestration.
caveat: The chapter calls the hard–soft tactic universal and notes that Deng could be abrasive while Huang could be conciliatory. The portraits are American-facing and partly impressionistic. Unresolved Mao–Zhou politics limit certainty about who directed every presentation.

claim: PRC officials use public communication around negotiations to establish agendas, raise or reduce expectations, advertise limits, and suggest openings, with different outlets offering different degrees of commitment.
evidence_type: Press interviews and statements; memcon excerpts; memoir descriptions of media arrangements; author inferences about audience effects.
historical_anchor: Carter–Deng, January 29, 1979; Deng–Kissinger, November 25, 1974; Deng–Ford, December 3, 1975; Haig–Huang Hua, October 30, 1981; Lin–Roy, July 25, 1978; Ji Chaozhu–U.S. Embassy Officer, March 2, 1982.
test: Connect public messages to private offers and identified audiences. Code outlet authority for the relevant period and distinguish agenda effects, domestic defense, expectation management, and actual concessions. Include instances of preserved confidentiality and publicity that releases pressure.
caveat: Solomon documents learning about television, failed expectation-raising, and respect for some confidentiality requests. The historical media hierarchy is not automatically valid later. His suggestion that a Chinese press criticism influenced the Mayaguez response is conjectural and needs independent causal evidence.

claim: Rapid collection and internal circulation of foreign reporting can inform PRC bargaining while also generating domestic reactions that constrain negotiators or intensify later responses.
evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; personal communications; press-based reconstruction of feedback; admitted uncertainty about editorial selection.
historical_anchor: Zhang Wenjin–Holdridge, January 11, 1982; Zhang–Freeman, September 9, 1981; Deng–Haig, June 16, 1981; Deng–Mondale, November 22, 1981; June–July 1983 coverage of arms-sales protests.
test: Trace what reporting reached which institutions, when, and with what interpretation. Compare foreign publication, Chinese internal circulation, subsequent official discussion, and policy response. Distinguish exposure to information from accurate understanding and from actual political constraint.
caveat: Solomon says the selection procedures for internal publications were unknown. Some feedback mechanisms rely on private explanations or chronological inference. Abundant access to information does not prove unfiltered reporting to leaders or correct interpretation of a foreign political system.

claim: PRC negotiators preserve and invoke the prior record, including protests and predecessors' words, but may restate disputed commitments in forms more favorable to their current position.
evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; comparison of communiqué wording and later paraphrases; press statements and rebuttals; cultural interpretation of political language.
historical_anchor: Deng–Vance, August 24, 1977; Haig–Huang Hua, October 23, 1981; Kissinger–Huang Zhen, January 8, 1977; Huang Hua–Woodcock, August 11, 1978; Han Nianlong–Woodcock, December 5, 1978; 1980–1981 dispute over alleged limits on Taiwan arms sales.
test: Compare original bilingual texts, oral records, later paraphrases, and explicit objections. Code whether a claimed obligation was accepted, unilateral, tacit, or contested. Track whether protests are later invoked rather than interpreting repetition as immediate escalation.
caveat: The chapter's translation and distortion allegations require checking against originals. Cultural claims about written Chinese do not independently explain document management. Table 2 is a set of contextual signaling hypotheses, not an automatic dictionary of intent. Solomon also acknowledges mutual overreading of symbols.

claim: Statements of independence, indifference, or foreign indebtedness can portray the counterpart as the party needing agreement and responsible for repairing the relationship.
evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; rhetorical analysis; author inference concerning dependence and bargaining psychology.
historical_anchor: Zhou–Kissinger, July 9–10, 1971; Qiao–Bush, November 4, 1975; Deng–Regan, November 19, 1981, on technology and the census computer.
test: Compare declarations of low need with private priorities, outside options, urgency, and costly actions. Separate evidenced grievances over prior undertakings from attempts to generate guilt. Test whether the counterpart changes its estimate of leverage or makes a concession.
caveat: Solomon interprets these claims through the relationship game and anxiety about dependence, but real asymmetries or genuine performance disputes may also explain them. Analyst disbelief is not a reliable measure of the speaker's actual valuation.

claim: PRC officials use challenges to the counterpart's resolve, logic, motives, and policy consistency to contest its rationale and encourage behavior favorable to Chinese interests.
evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; repeated rhetorical examples; author interpretations of intended policy effects.
historical_anchor: Kissinger–Qiao, October 8, 1976; Huang Hua–Brzezinski, May 21, 1978; Deng–Kissinger, October 20, 1975; Geng–Brown, January 7, 1980; Deng–Fulbright congressional delegation, September 5, 1974; Deng–Vance, August 24, 1977.
test: Code the specific criticism, the preceding foreign argument, factual merits, rebuttal, and subsequent offer or policy. Compare reciprocal use by the other side. Distinguish irritation or defensive speech from changes in negotiating behavior and final outcomes.
caveat: Kissinger sometimes rejected the premise explicitly, and Deng's debunking could resist perceived American pressure. The chapter's linkage to dialectical reasoning is interpretive; similar forms of persuasion are internationally familiar and may express sincere substantive disagreement.

claim: Openly specifying differences can coexist with limited cooperation, reassuring domestic and allied audiences while clarifying the common interests that sustain an agreement.
evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; Kissinger memoir account of communiqué drafting; comparative interpretation of three periods of tension.
historical_anchor: Mao–Kissinger, February 17–18, 1973; October 1971 Shanghai Communiqué drafting; Qiao–Bush, October 31, 1975; Deng–Ford, December 2, 1975.
test: Compare public disagreement with private cooperation, agreement language, and audience reassurance. Identify the point at which differentiation preserves a deal or leads to breakdown. Test shared interests rather than tone as a predictor of continuing cooperation.
caveat: Solomon distinguishes the domestic and strategic conditions of different episodes and credits compromise by both parties. The explanation does not imply that all harsh rhetoric is compatible with agreement or that disagreement is merely theatrical.

claim: Control over the schedule and apparent willingness to wait can help PRC negotiators exploit the counterpart's deadline, but Chinese negotiators are also susceptible to time pressure.
evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; memoir account of mutual deadline bargaining; comparison of Chinese, American, and British timing advantages.
historical_anchor: Huang Hua–Woodcock, July 5 and 14, 1978; Qiao–Kissinger, February 24–25, 1972; Carter–Chai Zemin, September 19, 1978; Vance–Huang Hua, October 3, 1978; abandoned February 28, 1982, target; PRC Hong Kong deadline announcement, November 9, 1983.
test: Identify who set each deadline, its credibility, who could walk away, timing of concessions, and consequences of expiry. Compare actual urgency with rhetoric of patience. Include deadlines ignored without agreement and cases in which Beijing faces greater time costs.
caveat: Kissinger described both sides using the 1972 deadline. The United States declined an unfavorable deal in February 1982, and Solomon recognizes initial British time leverage over Hong Kong. Cultural reserve does not establish an inherent Chinese advantage in patience.

claim: A shift toward concrete drafting and intervention by a senior PRC leader can signal that agreement is authorized and near, even after apparent deadlock.
evidence_type: Memoir descriptions; memcon-anchored cases; participant observations; an explicit aborted-agreement example.
historical_anchor: July 10–11, 1971, visit-announcement drafting; final Shanghai Communiqué discussions; Deng–Woodcock, December 13, 1978; Wan Li–Samuel Pierce, August 14, 1982; early 1984 nuclear cooperation discussions; PRC claims/assets message, June 14, 1974.
test: Date senior involvement relative to concessions, draft convergence, and final decisions. Include high-level encounters ending without agreement and agreements completed without a public leader intervention. Distinguish the leader authorizing compromise from blessing a deal already negotiated.
caveat: The chapter's face-based explanation is not independently established, and selected successful cases cannot determine reliability. Senior authority does not eliminate bureaucratic reversal: the chapter cites repudiation of the 1973 claims/assets solution. Several local date inconsistencies require original-source checking.

claim: Implementation can remain a bargaining arena in which PRC officials demand adherence from the counterpart while seeking adjustment, accommodation, or new concessions themselves.
evidence_type: Memcon references; narrative examples of implementation disputes and Chinese reversals; commercial complaints.
historical_anchor: Qiao–Bruce, April 2, 1974; normalization timing disputes; repudiated 1973 claims/assets arrangement; withdrawn 1981 Liu Huaqing visit; Zhao–Reagan grain-trade discussion in spring 1984; Deng–Brzezinski, May 21, 1978.
test: Create a bilateral obligation ledger distinguishing binding terms, political intentions, conditions, unilateral expectations, and later amendments. Assess actual performance, reasons for departure, requests for accommodation, and reciprocal concessions after signature.
caveat: The chapter mixes formal agreements with contemplated visits and expressions of intent; these are not equivalent commitments. Deng's May 1978 acknowledgment that a new administration could reconsider qualifies the claim of rigid continuity. Commercial complaints require independent evidence before generalization to political agreements.
